$comment: Curated, kid-friendly data. EVERY fact has `src` (file id in data-raw/sources) + `quote`/`quotes` (verbatim snippet). `npm run data` verifies the quotes and fails if one is not in the source. Missing facts are null -> shown as 'Data not available'. See README 'How to add a new machine'.

launchDate.quote: Launch date and time April 17, 1967 07:05:01 UT

launchSite.quote: Launch site Cape Canaveral, Florida Launch Complex 36B

purpose.value: Soft-land on the Moon and test its soil
purpose.quote: It tested the lunar surface and helped scientists determine that the ground was strong enough to support the weight of an Apollo Lunar Module

destination.quote: in the southeastern region of Oceanus Procellarum

abandoned.quote: May 4, 1967 Last contact with the spacecraft

location.name: Oceanus Procellarum
location.quote: at 3° south latitude and 23.41° west longitude

images.caption: Apollo 12 astronaut Pete Conrad standing next to the Surveyor 3 spacecraft.
images.quote: Apollo 12 astronaut Pete Conrad standing next to the Surveyor 3 spacecraft

events.title: Blast off!
events.text: Surveyor 3 launched on an Atlas Centaur rocket. For the first time, a Surveyor started from a “parking orbit” around Earth before its rocket stage fired it toward the Moon.
quotes: Unlike earlier Surveyor missions, Surveyor 3 began its journey from an Earth parking orbit
The Centaur upper stage then fired its engine to send the spacecraft toward the Moon
2,200 pounds (997.9 kilograms)

events.title: A bouncy landing
events.text: Shiny rocks confused the lander’s radar, so the engine did not switch off on time. Surveyor 3 bounced twice — first up to about 10 metres — before settling into a soft landing.
quotes: highly reflective rocks confused the lander's descent radar
Surveyor 3 bounced twice: first to about 33 feet (10 meters), then to about 10 feet (3 meters)
settled into a soft landing at 00:04:17 UT on April 20, 1967

events.title: Digging in moon dirt
events.text: Surveyor 3 was the first Surveyor with a scoop. It dug trenches and pushed on the ground. The soil was like wet sand — strong enough to hold an Apollo Lunar Module!
quotes: For the first time, a Surveyor carried a surface-sampling instrument
dig four trenches, perform four bearing tests, and conduct thirteen impact tests
lunar soil had a consistency similar to wet sand
Scientists concluded that the surface could support an Apollo Lunar Module
it sent 6,326 television pictures

events.title: Last message home
events.text: Earth heard from Surveyor 3 for the last time. The silent lander stayed where it was on the Moon.
events.quote: May 4, 1967 Last contact with the spacecraft

events.title: Astronauts come to visit!
events.text: More than three years later, Apollo 12 landed about 180 metres away. On their second moonwalk, astronauts Charles Conrad Jr. and Alan L. Bean walked over and took parts home — including the scoop and the camera.
details: Charles Conrad Jr. & Alan L. Bean
quotes: landed the Intrepid Lunar Module about 197 yards (180 meters) from the inactive Surveyor 3 spacecraft
During their second moonwalk on November 19, the astronauts visited the lander and brought back several parts, including the soil scoop and camera system

events.title: Space-weathered parts
events.text: Back on Earth, scientists studied the returned parts to learn how nearly two and a half years on the Moon had changed them.
events.quote: Scientists studied these components to learn how nearly two and a half years of exposure to the lunar environment had affected them

dataNotes: Conflict: the Surveyor 3 PDF says Apollo 12 landed on November 18, 1969 and visited on November 19; the NSSDCA Apollo 12 page gives 19 Nov 1969 (landing, UT) and 20 Nov 1969 (second moonwalk, UT). The gap is a time-zone difference (EST vs UT). Surveyor 3’s timeline follows the Surveyor 3 PDF; Apollo 12’s timeline follows NSSDCA.

machines.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module “Eagle”

launchSite.quote: Launch Site: Cape Canaveral, United States

purpose.value: Land the first astronauts on the Moon

events.title: Riding a Saturn 5
events.text: Eagle left Earth tucked on top of a giant Saturn 5 rocket from Cape Canaveral. Fully fuelled, the two-stage lander weighed 15,103 kg.
quotes: Launch Date: 1969-07-16
Launch Vehicle: Saturn 5
Mass: 15103 kg

events.title: “The Eagle has landed”
events.text: Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquility. Neil Armstrong radioed: “Houston, Tranquility Base here — the Eagle has landed.”
details: Neil A. Armstrong & Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin, Jr.
quotes: The LM landed at 20:17:40 UT (4:17:40 p.m. EDT) on 20 July 1969
Houston, Tranquility Base here - the Eagle has landed

events.title: One small step
events.text: Armstrong became the first person to step onto the Moon: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” Aldrin followed 19 minutes later and called it “Magnificent desolation”.
quotes: Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface at 02:56:15 UT on 21 July
That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind
Aldrin followed 19 minutes later, calling the lunar surface "Magnificent desolation"
collected 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil
The astronauts traversed a total distance of about 250 meters

events.title: Science left behind
events.text: The astronauts set up the EASEP: a solar-powered science station with a seismometer to feel moonquakes and a dust detector. A laser reflector was placed nearby too.
quotes: two solar panels to provide power (the EASEP could only operate during lunar day)
a passive seismometer, designed to measure seismic activity and physical properties of the lunar crust and interior, and a lunar dust detector
The unit had a total mass of 48 kg
The laser ranging retroreflector (LRRR) was also considered part of the EASEP

events.title: Goodbye, Moon
events.text: After 21 hours and 36 minutes, Eagle’s top half (the ascent stage) blasted off to rejoin Michael Collins. The bottom half stayed on the Moon — and it is still there.
quotes: The LM lifted off from the Moon at 17:54:01 UT on 21 July after 21 hours, 36 minutes on the lunar surface
After docking with the CSM, piloted by Michael Collins
The descent stage served as a platform for launching the ascent stage and was left behind on the Moon

events.title: A mystery ending
events.text: The empty ascent stage was let go in orbit around the Moon. Nobody knows exactly what happened to it — it is assumed to have crashed into the Moon within 1 to 4 months.
quotes: the LM was jettisoned into lunar orbit at 00:01:01 UT on 22 July
The fate of the LM is not known, but it is assumed that it crashed into the lunar surface sometime within the following 1 to 4 months

events.title: The science station goes quiet
events.text: Even though it got 30 °C hotter than planned, the EASEP worked normally. Near noon on its second lunar day it stopped accepting commands from Earth, and the experiment ended.
quotes: Despite operating temperatures which exceeded the planned maximum by 30 C the EASEP functioned normally
on 27 August 1969, near noon of this second lunar day, the EASEP no longer accepted commands from Earth stations and the experiment was terminated

dataNotes: The NSSDCA page does not name the launch pad, only “Cape Canaveral, United States”.

events.title: Second trip to the Moon
events.text: Intrepid launched on a Saturn 5 rocket. It would become the second crewed vehicle ever to land on the Moon.
quotes: Launch Date: 1969-11-14
was the second crewed vehicle to land on the Moon
Mass: 15235 kg

events.title: A pinpoint landing
events.text: Intrepid landed within about 180 metres of Surveyor 3, a robot lander that had been waiting there since April 1967. That is super accurate parking!
details: Charles P. “Pete” Conrad & Alan L. Bean
quotes: landed at 06:54:35 UT (1:54:35 a.m. EST) on 19 November 1969
within about 180 meters of the Surveyor 3 spacecraft, which had landed on April 20, 1967
Commander Charles P. "Pete" Conrad and LM pilot Alan L. Bean

events.title: Oops — the TV camera!
events.text: While it was being set up, the TV camera was accidentally pointed at the Sun. Its picture tube was damaged and the camera stopped working.
events.quote: The TV camera was inadvertantly pointed towards the Sun when it was being set up and the vidicon tube was damaged rendering the camera inoperable

events.title: Science station switched on
events.text: On the first moonwalk the astronauts set up the ALSEP, powered by a nuclear battery (an RTG) making about 70 watts. Its instruments listened for moonquakes and measured the solar wind and magnetism.
details: Seismometer, ion detector, ion gauge, dust detector, magnetometer, solar wind spectrometer
quotes: was turned on at 14:21 UT on 19 November 1969
The SNAP-27 model RTG produced the power to run the ALSEP operations
The RTG produced approximately 70 W DC at 16 V
a passive seismometer
a lunar surface magnetometer (LSM)
a solar wind spectrometer

events.title: Visiting Surveyor 3
events.text: On the second moonwalk they hiked 1.3 km, collecting rocks — and walked up to Surveyor 3! They brought about 10 kg of its parts back to Earth to study.
quotes: they completed a 1.3 km geology traverse, collecting samples and taking photographs, and visited the Surveyor 3 spacecraft , bringing back about 10 kg of parts for later examination on Earth
They collected a total of 34.35 kg of rock and soil samples

events.title: The first human-made moonquake
events.text: After 31 hours on the Moon the crew flew home in the top half. Then that empty ascent stage was crashed into the Moon on purpose, about 60 km from their seismometer — making the first recorded artificial moonquake!
details: about 60 km from the seismic station
quotes: The LM lifted off on 20 November at 14:25:47 UT (9:25 a.m. EST) after spending 31 hours 31 minutes on the Moon
intentionally crashed into the Moon
about 60 km from the seismic station at the Apollo 12 landing site, creating the first recorded artificial moonquake

events.title: Science station switched off
events.text: Nearly eight years later, the Apollo 12 ALSEP was shut down together with all the other Apollo science stations on the Moon.
events.quote: shut down along with the other ALSEP stations on 30 September 1977

dataNotes: The NSSDCA page does not name the launch pad, only “Cape Canaveral, United States”.

machines.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Module “Falcon”

launchSite.quote: Launch Site: Cape Canaveral, United States

purpose.value: Explore far with the first Moon buggy
quotes: The LM also carried a Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV)
This was the first time a vehicle of this type had been used

destination.quote: in the Mare Imbrium region at the foot of the Apennine mountain range

abandoned.note: descent stage left; ALSEP off in 1977

images.caption: Image of the Apollo 15 Lunar Module /ALSEP spacecraft.

events.title: Packing a car for the Moon
events.text: Falcon launched on a Saturn 5 carrying something new: a folded-up Lunar Roving Vehicle — a Moon buggy!
quotes: Launch Date: 1971-07-26
The LM also carried a Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV)
Mass: 16430 kg

events.title: Landing by the mountains
events.text: Falcon landed at the foot of the Apennine mountains with David R. Scott and James B. Irwin — the seventh and eighth people to walk on the Moon.
details: David R. Scott & James B. Irwin
quotes: landed at 22:16:29 UT (6:16:29 p.m. EDT) on 30 July 1971 in the Mare Imbrium region at the foot of the Apennine mountain range
Commander David R. Scott and LM pilot James B. Irwin, the seventh and eighth men to walk on the Moon

events.title: First drive on the Moon
events.text: On the first moonwalk the rover was unloaded and driven — the first time a vehicle like this was used. They drove 10.3 km to the edge of Hadley Rille and set up the ALSEP science station.
quotes: The first moonwalk EVA was on 31 July from 13:13:10 UT to 19:45:59 UT, during which time the LRV was unloaded, deployed, and driven
This was the first time a vehicle of this type had been used
The traverse on the first EVA covered 10.3 km to the edge of Hadley Rille to Elbow Crater
was turned on at 18:37 UT on 31 July 1971

events.title: Taking the Moon’s temperature
events.text: This ALSEP had seven instruments, including a new heat-flow experiment to measure how fast heat escapes from inside the Moon.
quotes: (7) a heat flow experiment, designed to measure the rate of heat loss from the lunar interior and the thermal properties of lunar material
The SNAP-27 model RTG produced the power to run the ALSEP operations

events.title: Hammer vs. feather
events.text: After the last moonwalk, Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on live TV. With no air on the Moon, they fell at the same rate!
quotes: Scott performed a televised demonstration of a hammer and feather falling at the same rate in the lunar vacuum
three moonwalk extra-vehicular activities (EVAs) totaling 18 hours, 35 minutes
During this time they covered 27.9 km and collected 77.31 kg of rock and soil samples

events.title: Leaving gifts behind
events.text: Before leaving, the crew placed a plaque and a small figure honouring the 14 American and Soviet space explorers who had died. Falcon’s top half lifted off after almost 67 hours on the Moon.
quotes: The astronauts also left a plaque and small figure on the surface in memory of all fourteen American and Soviet space explorers
The LM lifted off the Moon on 2 August at 17:11:22 UT after 66 hours, 55 minutes on the lunar surface

events.title: Crash landing (on purpose)
events.text: The empty ascent stage was released and hit the Moon about two hours later.
events.quote: the LM was jettisoned on 3 August at 01:04:14 UT and impacted on the Moon 2 hours later (03:03:37.0 UT) at 26.36 N, 0.25 E

events.title: Science station switched off
events.text: The Apollo 15 ALSEP was shut down along with all the other Apollo science stations.
events.quote: shut down along with the other ALSEP stations on 30 September 1977

dataNotes: The Lunar Roving Vehicle is described inside the Apollo 15 LM record; it has no separate record, launch data or image, so it is not a separate machine.

machines.name: Viking 1

launchDate.quote: Launch Date and Time Aug. 20, 1975 / 21:22:00 UT

launchSite.quote: Launch Site Cape Canaveral, Fla. / Launch Complex 41

purpose.value: Search Mars for signs of life
purpose.quote: collect evidence on the possibility on life on Mars

destination.quote: the western slopes of Chryse Planitia (Golden Plain)

quotes: Nov. 11, 1982 Lander stopped operating after getting a faulty command
Aug. 7, 1980 Orbiter was shut down after running out of attitude-control propellant

location.name: Chryse Planitia
location.quote: set down safely at 22.483 degrees north latitude and 47.94 degrees west longitude

events.title: A last-minute swap
events.text: Just before launch, the first spacecraft’s batteries ran down, so NASA swapped in the second one — which flew as Viking 1 on a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket.
quotes: Prior to launch, the batteries of the first spacecraft were discharged, prompting NASA to replace the original first spacecraft with the second, which was launched as Viking 1
7,776 pounds (3,527 kilograms)

events.title: Arriving at Mars
events.text: After three course corrections, Viking 1 went into orbit around Mars. It was really two machines in one: an orbiter and a lander riding together.
quotes: After three course corrections
the spacecraft entered orbit around Mars June 19, 1976
an orbiter (5,157 pounds or 2,339 kilograms) and a lander (2,156 pounds or 978 kilograms)

events.title: Too bumpy to land!
events.text: The orbiter’s first photos showed the planned landing site in Chryse was rougher than expected. Scientists used the new pictures to pick a safer spot.
quotes: scientists discovered that the area was rougher than expected
Using the new photos, scientists targeted the lander to a different site on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia (Golden Plain)

events.title: The first truly successful Mars landing
events.text: Viking Lander 1 set down safely — the first truly successful landing on Mars. It landed about 28 km from its target and soon sent colour photos and a 300° panorama.
quotes: NASA's Viking 1 made the first truly successful landing on Mars
Viking Lander 1 set down safely at 22.483 degrees north latitude and 47.94 degrees west longitude at 11:53:06 UT July 20, 1976
It landed about 17 miles (28 kilometers) from its planned target
a 300-degree panorama
minus 86 degrees Celsius
minus 33 degrees Celsius

events.title: A broken earthquake detector
events.text: Not everything worked: the lander’s seismometer, built to feel “marsquakes”, did not work.
events.quote: The seismometer on the lander was, however, inoperable

events.title: Is anything alive?
events.text: The robot arm scooped the first Martian soil into a tiny biology lab. Some tests looked like a weak “maybe” for life, but the main test for organic chemicals said no. The soil also had lots of sulfur.
quotes: On July 28, 1976, the lander's robot arm scooped up the first soil samples and deposited them into a special biological laboratory
could have been construed as indicating the presence of life (weak positive)
gave negative results
Data showed an abundance of sulfur

events.title: The orbiter runs out of fuel
events.text: After 1,489 orbits and many sharp photos of Mars and its two moons, the orbiter ran out of the gas it used to point itself and was switched off.
events.quote: was shut down Aug. 7, 1980, after it ran out of attitude control propellant on its 1,489th orbit around Mars

events.title: A new name
events.text: The lander kept sending weather reports. It was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station, honouring the leader of the Viking imaging team.
quotes: The lander continued to return daily (and then eventually weekly) weather reports
In January 1982, it was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station in honor of Thomas A. Mutch

events.title: One wrong command
events.text: A faulty command sent from Earth cut off communications. Engineers tried to get back in touch, but they never could. The lander is still sitting on Mars.
quotes: The lander operated until Nov. 11, 1982, when a faulty command sent from Earth resulted in an interruption of communications
Further attempts to regain contact proved to be unsuccessful

dataNotes: Viking 1 is shown as one machine with two markers (lander on the surface at the given coordinates, plus a stylised orbiter circling Mars).
The image totals in the PDF (52,663 orbiter images; 4,500 lander photos) are for BOTH Viking missions together, so they are not shown as Viking 1 numbers.

machines.name: Mars Pathfinder & Sojourner

launchSite.value: Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida
launchSite.quote: Launch location Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida, USA

purpose.value: Test new ways to land and rove on Mars
purpose.quote: Mars Pathfinder was designed as a technology demonstration to deliver an instrumented lander and a free-ranging robotic rover to the surface of Mars

abandoned.quote: before its final data transmission on September 27, 1997

events.title: Off to Mars
events.text: Mars Pathfinder launched on a Delta II rocket, carrying a lander and a tiny rover. It was a test mission to try out new landing and driving technology.
details: Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida
quotes: Launch December 4, 1996 (UTC)
Rocket Delta II 7925
Sojourner 23 pounds (10.6 kilograms)
while testing new landing and surface-operation technologies

events.title: Bounce, bounce, bounce!
events.text: A parachute slowed it down, then giant airbags wrapped the lander like bubble wrap. It hit Mars at about 14 m/s and bounced about 15 times — up to 15 m high — the first airbag landing on Mars!
quotes: A large airbag system cushioned the impact—the first use of this landing technique on Mars
struck the surface at about 31 mph (14 meters per second)
about 19 feet (5.8 meters) in diameter
Pathfinder bounced about 15 times, reaching heights of up to 50 feet (15 meters)

events.title: Sojourner rolls out
events.text: On sol 2 (the second Martian day), the rover Sojourner stood up to its full height of about 30 cm and rolled down the lander’s ramp onto Mars. It was named after civil-rights activist Sojourner Truth.
quotes: Late on July 5, 1997 (sol 2, the second Martian day), Sojourner rose to its full height of about 1 foot (30 centimeters) and rolled down the lander's rear ramp, which was inclined at 20 degrees
named after American civil-rights activist Sojourner Truth
The lander was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station

events.title: Clues of ancient water
events.text: Rounded pebbles and cobbles hinted at rocks formed by flowing water. Mars may once have been warmer and wetter!
quotes: Rounded pebbles and cobbles suggested conglomerate rocks formed by flowing water
Findings suggested Mars may once have been warmer and wetter, with liquid water at the surface
Ares Vallis is an ancient floodplain
completed more than 15 chemical analyses of rocks and soil

events.title: Dust devils & magnetic dust
events.text: Weather sensors caught dust devils swirling by, the floating dust turned out to be magnetic, and thin water-ice clouds showed up early in the morning.
quotes: Temperature, wind, and pressure sensors measured dust devils
Airborne dust was magnetic
Its properties suggested the mineral could be maghemite
Early-morning water-ice clouds were observed in the lower atmosphere

events.title: Final message
events.text: Pathfinder sent its last data. In total it returned 2.3 billion bits of information, including more than 16,500 lander pictures and 550 rover pictures.
quotes: Mars Pathfinder returned about 2.3 billion bits of information before its final data transmission on September 27, 1997
It sent more than 16,500 lander images and 550 rover images

dataNotes: Exact landing coordinates are not in the data (only “Ares Vallis”). The marker uses an approximate display position, labelled as approximate in the app.

Sojourner has no separate end date in the data, so the lander + rover are one machine (the uploaded rover 3D model represents Sojourner). The rover model is a generic rover by shriyans716 (CC-BY-4.0) and does not look exactly like the real Sojourner.
The data gives no launch time or launch pad number.

machines.name: NEAR Shoemaker

launchDate.quote: Launch Date and Time Feb. 17, 1996 / 20:43:27 UT

launchSite.quote: Launch Site Cape Canaveral, Fla. / Launch Complex 17B

purpose.value: Orbit and study the asteroid Eros
purpose.quote: NEAR's primary goal was to rendezvous with the minor planet 433 Eros

destination.quote: the minor planet 433 Eros (an S-class asteroid)

abandoned.quote: Last contact with NEAR was Feb. 28, 2001

events.title: A low-cost explorer
events.text: NEAR was the very first mission of NASA’s Discovery program — smaller, cheaper science missions. It was also the first spacecraft to run on solar power beyond the orbit of Mars.
quotes: was the first mission flown under NASA's Discovery program
The spacecraft was the first to rely on solar cells for power during operations beyond Mars orbit
1,775 pounds (805 kilograms)

events.title: Say hi to Mathilde
events.text: On the way, NEAR zoomed past asteroid 253 Mathilde for 25 minutes. It turned out to be covered in craters and less dense than expected.
quotes: NEAR performed a 25-minute flyby of the asteroid 253 Mathilde on June 27, 1997
The closest approach was about 750 miles (1,200 kilometers)
the spacecraft photographed 60 percent of the minor planet
is covered with craters and is less dense than previously believed

events.title: A slingshot from Earth
events.text: NEAR swung past Earth, using our planet’s gravity like a slingshot to head toward Eros.
quotes: NEAR flew by Earth on Jan. 23, 1998, at 07:23 UT for a gravity assist on its way to Eros
The closest approach was about 335 miles (540 kilometers)

events.title: Engine trouble!
events.text: An engine burn was aborted, so NEAR missed the steering it needed to meet Eros. The team switched to a backup plan.
quotes: an aborted engine burn on Dec. 20, 1998, that prevented a critical trajectory correction
NEAR was put on a backup trajectory

events.title: First look at Eros
events.text: NEAR flew past Eros and saw about 60% of it. Eros was smaller than expected, with two medium-sized craters and a long ridge.
quotes: the spacecraft first flew past Eros on Dec. 23, 1998
2,380 miles (3,827 kilometers)
it observed about 60 percent of the asteroid, and discovered that the minor planet was smaller than expected
the asteroid has two medium-sized craters, a long surface ridge

events.title: First asteroid orbiter ever
events.text: About a year late, NEAR finally moved into orbit around Eros — the first human-made object ever to orbit an asteroid. A Valentine’s Day first!
quotes: NEAR finally moved into orbit around Eros at 15:33 UT Feb. 14, 2000, roughly a year later than intended, becoming the first human-made object to orbit a minor planet
200 × 225 miles (321 × 366 kilometers)

events.title: Named after a rock star (geologist)
events.text: NASA renamed the spacecraft NEAR Shoemaker in honour of the famous geologist Eugene M. Shoemaker.
events.quote: on March 14, 2000, a month after entering asteroid orbit, NASA renamed the NEAR spacecraft NEAR Shoemaker in honor of Eugene M. Shoemaker

events.title: Power surge
events.text: Controllers had to turn off the near-infrared spectrometer because of a big power surge.
events.quote: on May 13, 2000, controllers had to turn off the near-infrared spectrometer due to an excessive power surge

events.title: Landing on an asteroid!
events.text: NEAR wasn’t built to land — but it slowly came down, taking 69 close-up photos, and touched Eros at a gentle 6.4 km/h. It survived and kept sending data for about two weeks!
quotes: the spacecraft – which was not designed as a lander – survived touchdown on the asteroid and returned valuable data for about two weeks

during which it took 69 high-resolution photos of Eros, NEAR touched down on Eros at a gentle 4 miles per hour (6.4 kilometers per hour), just south of a saddle-shaped feature named Himeros, on Feb. 12, 2001, at 19:44 UT

events.title: Frozen silent
events.text: In the extreme cold of −173 °C, NEAR stopped talking. By then it had sent about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 pictures — and found that Eros has no magnetic field.
quotes: The last contact with NEAR was Feb. 28, 2001, the spacecraft having succumbed to the extreme cold
minus 173 degrees Celsius
The spacecraft returned about 10 times more data than originally planned, including 160,000 images
NEAR data showed that Eros had no magnetic field

events.title: Anyone there?
events.text: Nearly two years later, NASA tried to contact NEAR again. There was no answer.
events.quote: NASA's attempt to contact the probe nearly two years later on Dec. 10, 2002, was unsuccessful

dataNotes: NEAR sits on Eros, which is shown as a stylised, procedurally generated asteroid. Its position in the scene is decorative, not a real orbit.

machines.name: Kepler Space Telescope

purpose.value: Hunt for Earth-size planets around other stars
purpose.quote: became the agency's first mission to detect Earth-size planets in the habitable zones of their stars

abandoned.quote: Before retiring the spacecraft on Oct. 30, 2018

events.title: The biggest camera in space
events.text: Kepler launched with the largest digital camera sent into space for observing at that time. Its job: stare at about 150,000 stars in the constellation Cygnus.
quotes: Launched on March 6, 2009
the largest digital camera outfitted for outer space observations at that time
stare continuously at 150,000 stars in one star-studded patch of the sky in the constellation Cygnus
3-foot (1-meter) diameter aperture telescope
4 feet, 7 inches (1.4 meters)

events.title: Five new worlds
events.text: Kepler finds planets by watching for tiny dips in a star’s brightness when a planet passes in front. In its first six weeks it found five — announced in January 2010.
quotes: Kepler detected planets by observing transits, or tiny dips in the brightness of a star that occur when a planet crosses in front of the star
During its first six weeks of operation, Kepler discovered five exoplanets—named Kepler 4b, 5b, 6b, 7b and 8b (which NASA announced in January 2010)

events.title: A family of planets
events.text: Kepler-9 became the first confirmed system with more than one planet passing in front of the same star.
quotes: In April 2010, mission scientists published results that showed that Kepler had discovered the first confirmed planetary system with more than one planet transiting the same star, Kepler-9
surveying more than 156,000 stars over a period of seven months

events.title: Six planets at Kepler-11
events.text: Around Kepler-11, a yellow dwarf star about 2,000 light years away, Kepler found six planets — all bigger than Earth.
quotes: The planetary system orbiting Kepler-11, a yellow dwarf star about 2,000 light years from Earth, included six planets
NASA announced in February 2011 that these planets were larger than Earth

events.title: A broken wheel
events.text: Kepler lost the second of its four reaction wheels (spinning wheels that aim the telescope). It needed three, so it could no longer stay pointed — ending the original mission.
quotes: In May 2013, the Kepler spacecraft lost the second of four gyroscope-like reaction wheels
effectively ending new data collection for the original mission
The spacecraft required three functioning wheels to position the telescope

events.title: K2: steering with sunlight
events.text: Engineers had a clever idea: use the push of sunlight to keep Kepler steady, like a kayak steering into the current. The new “K2” mission was expected to do 10 campaigns — it did 19!
quotes: using the pressure of sunlight to maintain its pointing, like a kayak steering into the current
the Kepler team estimated that the K2 mission could conduct 10 campaigns with the remaining fuel; it reached 19
bumped Kepler's count of surveyed stars up to more than 500,000

events.title: Retired with a full tank of discoveries
events.text: Running low on fuel, Kepler was retired. Its data suggest that 20 to 50% of the stars we can see at night may have small, possibly rocky planets in their habitable zones.
quotes: Before retiring the spacecraft on Oct. 30, 2018
even after initial warnings of low fuel
20 to 50 percent of the stars visible in the night sky are likely to have small, possibly rocky, planets similar in size to Earth, and located within the habitable zone
the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in April 2018

dataNotes: Missing in the data: launch site, launch vehicle and where Kepler is now (its orbit/destination). Shown as “Data not available”.
